# SnapDisk

> SnapDisk is a free Android app that backs up photos and videos to a USB disk. Plug in a USB disk, tap Backup in the notification, and photos copy oldest-first in the background — no account, no cloud, no ads. Free core (manual backup, 5 GB per run); SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase for auto-backup on disk connect and unlimited backup size.

## Download

- [Download SnapDisk v0.1.2 (APK, 11 MB)](https://github.com/dzianisv/photo-backup/releases/download/v0.1.2/app-release.apk): free Android app, needs Android 7.0 or later. Not on Google Play yet.
- [All releases](https://github.com/dzianisv/photo-backup/releases): every shipped version with its APK.

## About

- [SnapDisk landing page](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/): what it does, how it works, pricing, FAQ.
- [Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/dzianisv/photo-backup): Kotlin + Jetpack Compose, Material 3.
- [Privacy Policy](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/privacy.html): collects nothing — no account, no analytics, no ads, no internet permission.

the Agni 2 5G&#x27;s microSD slot is two things — a hybrid slot per smartprix and an expandable 256 GB dedicated slot per Flipkart, no slot at all per mobiledokan and mysmartprice — so check the tray on your unit before buying a card; the Agni 3 5G&#x27;s microSD slot is two things too — no slot at all per smartprix, GSMArena, notebookcheck and techspecs, a dedicated or hybrid slot per phonepik — so the same check applies, and the weight of the sources says no slot; the Blaze X 5G&#x27;s microSD slot is two things — no slot per smartprix and mysmartprice, a microSDXC slot per gsmfind; the Yuva 2&#x27;s second camera is two things — an 8 MP ultrawide per phonepik, a VGA sensor per smartprix; the Yuva 3 Pro&#x27;s second camera is two things — a 0.3 MP auxiliary lens per beebom, an 8 MP ultrawide per phonepik; the Yuva 2 Pro&#x27;s microSD ceiling is two numbers — up to 256 GB per 91mobiles, gadgetsnow and smartprix, with bajajfinserv listing the ceiling as not available; VaultDrive needs Android 8 or later per its own site, so every covered Lava phone clears it — and AppBrain lists 12.1 or later, which twelve of the fourteen clear — the Yuva 2 and Yuva 2 Pro run Android 12, below 12.1; no source found names the stock file manager on a Lava phone, so Method 2 uses Files by Google or the built-in file manager, whatever it is called on your unit; no source found states a microSD ceiling for the Blaze 2 5G, the Yuva 3 or the Yuva 3 Pro at all — only that they take microSD — so check the card slot on your unit before buying a card larger than 256 GB for any of those three; - [Back up photos from a broken-screen phone to USB](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/broken-screen-photos-to-usb.html): A broken screen is three different problems, and only two of them have a phone-to-USB route at all: a cracked screen with dead touch, where you can still see the display; a black screen with the phone still powering on, where you cannot see anything; and a completely dead phone, where no software route exists. This article covers all three, in that order, and it is the first article in this series that is about a situation instead of a phone brand — the brand series ran to 134 articles, and a broken screen can happen to any of them. Eighteen honest caveats up front: the three scenarios need three different routes, and only the first two have a phone-to-USB route at all; an OTG mouse unlocks nothing by itself — it only lets you enter your own PIN or pattern with a cursor, and it needs a screen you can still see; one port holds either the mouse or the drive, not both — a multi-port OTG hub, or Pro&#x27;s auto-backup on connect, is what lets mouse and drive share the port; video-out needs DisplayPort Alt Mode — a USB 2.0 port physically cannot carry video, and most budget phones lack it; Samsung DeX is the best-documented video-out route — the S8 and later S series, the Note 8 and later, all Z Fold models and the A90 5G only — while the Z Flip 5 and 6 output video but run no DeX, per XDA, and the rest of the A series outputs nothing; Pixel video-out starts at the Pixel 8 — the Pixel 6 and 7 have USB 3.x ports but Google left display output switched off until the Pixel 8; OnePlus video-out is contested — the 12, 13 and Open per the usbctohdmi guide, against the 7 and newer flagships per the salivity list — so check your exact model before buying a hub; Motorola&#x27;s desktop mode is Ready For, now Smart Connect, on Edge phones, and Huawei&#x27;s is Easy Projection on Mate and P Pro phones; an on-screen prompt can block video-out — if you cannot see or tap it, the hub route stops there; Android 16&#x27;s native desktop mode is rolling out — Pixel 8, 9 and 10 with Android 16 QPR3 or later, per Rayneo — so an older Pixel mirrors instead of opening a desktop; a completely dead phone has no software route — Android Authority says so plainly — and screen replacement or professional recovery is what is left; a microSD card comes out only if the phone takes one — most high-end phones no longer do, per Android Authority — and reading the card still needs a reader and a computer; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — one notification tap, which the mouse can do — and Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect, but only if it was set up before the screen broke; drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README; check Google Photos first — the library may already be safe in the cloud — but Storage saver compresses photos, so check that setting before trusting a cloud copy; iPhones are not covered here — SnapDisk is Android only — and the iPhone OTG route varies by model, per the repair-shop guide; and the search results for this query are four results — an Android Authority generic broken-phone recovery guide, a repair-shop guide that does mention OTG-mouse unlock and copying photos to a USB drive, and two Dr.Fone guides — none of them is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup guide for a broken screen, and none of them mentions SnapDisk. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.
- [Back up photos to USB when switching to a new phone](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/switching-phones-photos-to-usb.html): A new phone is the moment most people find out whether their photos were really backed up. The transfer usually works — but "usually" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and if the old phone has already been wiped or handed back for trade-in, there is no second chance. This article is about the step that comes before the transfer: a checked copy of the whole photo library on a USB drive you hold in your hand, made on the old phone, with no computer — and what to check before the old phone goes. Fourteen honest caveats up front: the exact query DOES return a switching-specific guide — coticsy.com's "How to Back Up Your Photos Before Switching to a New Phone" — it covers the switch generally and USB copy as one manual step (exFAT, Files app, manual select/copy), and it is the best guide in the results; SnapDisk's own generic guides (transfer-photos-to-usb-automatically, usb-photo-backup) and FotoSafe's generic guide and a YouTube manual-OTG video also surface; NONE of them is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup guide framed for the phone-switch moment, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills; SnapDisk is Android-only, so the iPhone half of a switch is the manual copy or a rival app, not SnapDisk; a transfer moves data, it is not a backup — it can be interrupted, skip items, or depend on photos that are not actually on the old phone because they live only in the cloud; the cloud-only originals trap is real in both directions — iCloud Photos with Optimize iPhone Storage keeps space-saving versions on the phone and the originals in iCloud, and Google Photos with Storage saver compresses photos larger than 16 MP down to 16 MP and videos over 1080p down to 1080p, per Google's own support page — so download the originals first; an exact file copy preserves the capture dates and locations already embedded in the originals, per the coticsy guide; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice — and Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit; drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README — so use exFAT if both phones support it, and test the drive with both phones before the switch; SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — the wipe step is always yours, and always after the check; and the search results for this query are five results — SnapDisk's own generic guide, the coticsy switching guide, SnapDisk's generic USB guide, FotoSafe's generic guide, and a YouTube manual-OTG video — none of them is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup guide framed for the phone-switch moment. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.
- [Back up photos from an SD card to USB (no computer)](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/sd-card-photos-to-usb.html): Your photos may live on a card, not in the phone — on the microSD card in the phone's slot, or on the full-size SD card in your camera. Either way the copy to a USB drive can be made with the phone alone, no computer — but the two cards are not the same job, and the guides that already exist only cover one of them. Fourteen honest caveats up front: the exact query DOES return real guides — five of them — brightideaphotography.com, desnoulez.fr, petapixel.com, Ask Tim Grey, and goldenlenstraveler.com; all five are about a camera's memory card copied to an SSD with the phone as a bridge, by hand in the Files app; none of them is about the phone's own microSD card; none of them is a whole-library one-tap backup; and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills; "SD card" means two different things here — the microSD card in your phone and the full-size SD card in your camera — and this article covers the phone's card first, then the camera's card; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice — and Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit; the From folder is a picker, not a fixed path — tap it, browse to the card, and choose the card's DCIM folder, which the picker reaches because it is the system folder picker, verified in the repo as OpenDocumentTree; drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README — so use exFAT, which the bridge guides recommend too; one USB port holds either the card reader or the drive, not both — copying straight from card to drive needs a powered hub, or two steps through the phone's storage; SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — the card stays a second copy until you have opened photos on the drive and checked them; an iPhone has no microSD slot, so the phone's-card route is Android only, and the camera-card route on iPhone is the Files app, not SnapDisk; and a card formatted by a camera may use a folder layout other than DCIM — check the card's folders before picking, and pick the folder that actually holds the photos. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.
- [Back up photos from a tablet to USB (no computer)](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/tablet-photos-to-usb.html): A tablet is not a big phone when it comes to backup — its library is often years of family photos, many Android tablets have a microSD slot that high-end phones no longer do, older tablets still use micro-USB while newer ones use USB-C, and whether the tablet supports USB OTG varies by model. The copy itself is the same job — tablet to drive, no computer — but the port, the slot, and the size change the steps. the phone-bridge pattern from the SD-card article does not apply the same way — the tablet holds the photos itself, so the copy is direct tablet-to-drive, and the bridge only reappears for a camera card; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice — and Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit; SnapDisk&#x27;s copy runs as a foreground service — the mechanism Android gives a copy that must keep running with the screen off — but the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no low-battery run has ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified, and this article says so instead of promising it; the drive occupies the phone&#x27;s only USB-C port — the phone cannot charge from a power bank at the same time unless the connection goes through a USB-C hub with pass-through charging, which is standard USB-C behaviour but unverified with SnapDisk; drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README — so use exFAT; a cloud backup is the slow way out of a low battery — it needs Wi-Fi, upload time, and free space in the account, and the phone burns battery uploading for hours; and SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — the phone stays a second copy until you have opened photos on the drive and checked them. - [Back up photos to USB before your Android update](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/android-update-photos-to-usb.html): Your phone is offering an Android update, and the update itself almost never wipes your photos — but a failed or stuck update, a bootloop, or a factory reset during troubleshooting does, and after a wipe there is no undo. Fifteen honest caveats up front: the exact query DOES return real guides — five of them — FotoSafe&#x27;s guided app backup, mefmobile.org, a YouTube OTG guide, umatechnology.org, and Dr.Fone&#x27;s four-method guide — and none of the five is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup framed for the before-an-Android-update moment, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills; the backup must COMPLETE and be verified on the drive BEFORE the update starts — a copy still running when the phone restarts for the update is not a backup, and there is no undo after a wipe; cloud-only originals are a trap — Google Photos backup can be off, device folders like WhatsApp and screenshots may never have been switched on, and storage saver uploads are compressed copies, not originals, so check photos.google.com before trusting the cloud — and with no Wi-Fi the upload cannot run at all, so the drive copy comes first and the cloud check waits for Wi-Fi; one USB-C port holds the drive OR the charger, not both — charge first, or use a powered hub with pass-through charging, which is standard USB-C behaviour but unverified with SnapDisk; a portable SSD may need a powered hub — the phone alone may not supply enough power for both the hub and the drive; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice — and Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit; the screenshot below is from SnapDisk on a phone — it is the same settings screen you will see, because this article is about a phone; the From folder is a picker, not a fixed path — tap it, browse to the phone&#x27;s storage, and choose the folder that holds the photos, which the picker reaches because it is the system folder picker, verified in the repo as OpenDocumentTree; drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README — so use exFAT; a spinning hard drive may need its own power; SnapDisk&#x27;s copy runs as a foreground service — the mechanism Android gives a copy that must keep running with the screen off — but the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no pre-update run has ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified, and this article says so instead of promising it; Android 15 and later give a dataSync foreground service 6 hours in 24 hours — if the copy runs past that, Android pauses it, and opening the app resets the timer; and SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — the phone stays a second copy until you have opened photos on the drive and checked them, and the drive stays unplugged while the update runs. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.
- [SnapDisk blog](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/blog/): how to back up photos to a USB drive on Android — no cloud, no account, no upload. Every post lives in the SnapDisk GitHub repo, version-controlled.
- [SnapDisk blog RSS feed](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/feed.xml): all blog posts as RSS.

## Support

- [Report an issue](https://github.com/dzianisv/photo-backup/issues): every report gets an answer.
- [Back up photos to USB from a water-damaged phone](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/water-damage-photos-to-usb.html): Your phone got wet and it still turns on — that is the narrow window, and it may be minutes, not hours: corrosion starts within hours, and a phone that works now may not turn on tomorrow, and after it dies there is no software route left, only a recovery lab. The honest caveats, up front: the exact query DOES return real guides — seven of them — alibaba.com&#x27;s generic local-backup guide, mdrepairs.com&#x27;s water-damage recovery lab, Wondershare Recoverit&#x27;s water-damage recovery guide, therepairdepot.com&#x27;s broken-phone recovery guide, gbtimes.com&#x27;s broken-phone transfer guide, MobileTrans&#x27;s recover-or-back-up-to-PC guide, and topselect.ca&#x27;s USB-C drive backup guide — and none of the seven frames a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup for the water-damage moment, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills; do NOT charge a wet phone and do NOT plug anything into a wet USB port — power through a damaged board can burn out the chip that holds the photos, and the lab&#x27;s own first step is power it off immediately and do not turn it back on to &quot;check&quot; it — so this article&#x27;s one-tap route is only for a phone that is on, working normally, and has a dry port, and the moment anything glitches, stops, or smells wrong, the copy stops, the phone goes off, and the lab takes over; if the phone is off or dead there is NO software route — only a recovery lab, and a lab is a per-case job, not a free app; the backup must COMPLETE and be verified on the drive before the phone dies — a copy still running when the phone dies is not a backup, and there is no undo after; cloud-only originals are a trap — Google Photos backup can be off, device folders like WhatsApp and screenshots may never have been switched on, and storage saver uploads are compressed copies, not originals, so check photos.google.com before trusting the cloud — and with no Wi-Fi the upload cannot run at all, so the drive copy comes first and the cloud check waits for Wi-Fi; one USB-C port holds the drive OR the charger, not both — and a wet phone must not be charged anyway, so the copy runs on the battery the phone has left, or through a powered hub with pass-through charging, which is standard USB-C behaviour but unverified with SnapDisk; a portable SSD may need a powered hub — the phone alone may not supply enough power for both the hub and the drive; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice — and Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit; the screenshot below is from SnapDisk on a phone — it is the same settings screen you will see, because this article is about a phone; the From folder is a picker, not a fixed path — tap it, browse to the phone&#x27;s storage, and choose the folder that holds the photos, which the picker reaches because it is the system folder picker, verified in the repo as OpenDocumentTree; drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README — so use exFAT; a spinning hard drive may need its own power; SnapDisk&#x27;s copy runs as a foreground service — the mechanism Android gives a copy that must keep running with the screen off — but the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no water-damage run has ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified, and this article says so instead of promising it; Android 15 and later give a dataSync foreground service 6 hours in 24 hours — if the copy runs past that, Android pauses it, and opening the app resets the timer; and SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — the phone stays a second copy until you have opened photos on the drive and checked them, and the drive stays dry and separate from the phone once the copy is done. - [Back up photos to USB before rooting your phone](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/rooting-photos-to-usb.html): Your phone is about to be unlocked and flashed, and it holds the only copy of months of photos — unlocking the bootloader wipes everything by design, and after the wipe there is no recovery. The honest caveats, up front: the exact query DOES return real guides — five of them — UMA Technology&#x27;s backup-before-flashing checklist, PrivacyPortal&#x27;s bootloader guide, Sod Calculator&#x27;s custom-ROM guide, Awesome Android Root&#x27;s unlock guide, and RottenWifi&#x27;s unlock guide — and all five frame backup as a step inside a flashing or unlock guide, with computer, cloud, or manual-copy routes — and none of the five is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup framed for the before-unlock moment, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills; unlocking the bootloader wipes ALL data BY DESIGN — the backup must COMPLETE and be verified on the drive BEFORE the unlock command runs, because after the wipe there is no recovery; SnapDisk backs up photos and videos ONLY — it does not back up app data, authenticator seeds, messages, or system state — so export authenticators, back up chats, and take a TWRP nandroid for a full system image separately; unplug the USB drive before flashing — the USB port is needed for the computer and fastboot — and keep the drive aside until the new ROM boots; unlocking may void the warranty, can break Play Integrity and banking apps, and some carrier variants cannot be unlocked at all — check before you start; rooting is NOT a factory reset or a repair — the wipe is deliberate and the phone then runs new software, not the stock system; cloud-only originals are a trap — Google Photos backup can be off, device folders like WhatsApp and screenshots may never have been switched on, and storage saver uploads are compressed copies, not originals, so check photos.google.com before trusting the cloud; this route is only for a phone that still works and has a dry, undamaged port — never plug anything into a damaged port, and a dead phone is a repair-lab job only; one USB-C port holds the drive OR the charger, not both — charge first, or use a powered hub with pass-through charging, which is standard USB-C behaviour but unverified with SnapDisk; - [SnapDisk vs FotoSafe: back up Android photos to USB](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/snapdisk-vs-fotosafe.html): SnapDisk vs FotoSafe — free trial, price, copy order, and verification, compared from the verified facts, as of November 2026.
- [SnapDisk vs Buffalo Photo Backup: Android USB backup](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/snapdisk-vs-buffalo.html): SnapDisk vs Buffalo Photo Backup — price, free tier, auto-backup, restore, and verification, compared from verified facts, as of November 2026.
- [Back up RAW photos to USB from Android — SnapDisk](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/raw-photos-to-usb.html): A RAW file is the negative — recompress it once and the edit is gone for good. SnapDisk copies .dng files byte-for-byte with no recompression, the certain route is picking the source folder with the From picker (.dng and .raw are in the recognised extension list), the free version covers 5 GB per run and Pro is $9.99 once, and the drive should be exFAT. Screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified.
- [Back up HEIC photos to USB from Android — SnapDisk](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/heic-photos-to-usb.html): A HEIC file is the smaller original — convert it to JPG once and the extra quality is gone for good. SnapDisk copies .heic files byte-for-byte with no conversion, the certain route is picking the source folder with the From picker (.heic and .heif are in the recognised extension list), the free version covers 5 GB per run and Pro is $9.99 once, and the drive should be exFAT. Screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified. Windows, the Photo Backup Stick and Google Photos Storage saver all convert HEIC to JPG — the backup must not.
- [Back up screenshots to USB from Android — SnapDisk](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/screenshots-to-usb.html): Screenshots live outside DCIM — Pictures/Screenshots on most phones, DCIM/Screenshots on Samsung — and the default run includes every .png byte-for-byte, while picking DCIM as From would miss them on most phones. If the phone truly has no host mode, copy via a computer (phone to computer by cable on File transfer/MTP, then computer to drive — the most dependable method per rottenwifi and mobiletrans, and the Windows-PC method in sekin.in), via a Wi-Fi flash drive (SanDisk Connect Wireless Stick, 2015 product whose companion apps SanDisk has been retiring — check the app is still available before buying), or via a different phone that does support OTG (Quick Share the photos across, then run SnapDisk there). VaultDrive needs OTG too — its Android route is headed "with OTG" — Pro $19.99 once, free up to 200 files or 2 GB, 2,000+ installs across both stores, re-verified live this run. - [Back up photos to an NTFS USB drive from Android — SnapDisk](https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/ntfs-photos-to-usb.html): Most Android phones can't write to an NTFS drive — Android has no native NTFS write support, so most phones won't mount one at all and the rest often mount it read-only. Check the format first (Windows: right-click the drive, Properties; on the phone: the drive's Properties in a USB file-manager app), then reformat to exFAT — which erases the drive, so copy its contents off first, and has no 4 GB file limit — or keep NTFS and copy by hand with an NTFS-writer app (Paragon exFAT/NTFS for USB, SAF document provider with NTFS as an in-app purchase; NTFS Reader, NTFS read free and NTFS write a one-time in-app purchase, exFAT/FAT32 read and write free; USB File Manager, read/write NTFS, exFAT, FAT32 and ext4, manual import; AnExplorer, reads/writes NTFS without root) — manual file-manager copy, no automation. SnapDisk's one-tap copy needs a writable drive: the app has no NTFS code at all and no read-only-mount check, verified in the code — on a drive the phone does not mount, no backup offer appears; on a drive mounted read-only, the first file's write is refused, the file is recorded in the skipped list with its full error, the job moves on, and the run ends with every file skipped and nothing copied, with no retry (retry-once fires only on size-verification failures) and no "drive is read-only" message. Whether a given phone mounts an NTFS drive read-only or not at all is unverified — no real-disk test of SnapDisk against an NTFS drive has been run. VaultDrive needs a writable drive too — its Android route is headed "with OTG", it recommends exFAT and warns about FAT32 — Pro $19.99 once, free up to 200 files or 2 GB, 2,000+ installs across both stores, re-verified live this run. The default run copies the whole MediaStore library, not DCIM only. The free version covers 5 GB per run and Pro is $9.99 once. Screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified. No top search result gives the check plus the three routes plus the honest statement that SnapDisk's one-tap run needs a writable drive in one guide — the results are NTFS-writer apps that copy by hand, or format explainers that never get to the backup.

A secondary user is a full user, not a restricted profile: it works on phones and tablets, signs in with its own Google account, and installs its own apps — the guest-profile routes are the temporary-borrower equivalent, the restricted-profile routes the tablet equivalent. Screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified. No top search result offers a phone-direct USB-drive backup of secondary-user photos — the generic OTG guides never mention a secondary user, and the secondary-user explainers never take the USB step.
